# The Quiet Art of Getting Lost

There's something I've been thinking about lately, something that doesn't quite fit into the compartmentalized boxes we usually reserve for important thoughts. It's about getting lost—not the panic-inducing, stuck-in-an-unfamiliar-city kind of lost, though there's that too—but the deliberate, almost meditative kind of lostness that seems increasingly rare in our world of GPS coordinates and real-time location sharing.

I remember the last time I was genuinely, completely lost. I was nineteen, driving through New Mexico with a friend, and somewhere between Gallup and the Arizona border, we took what we thought was a shortcut. The road got progressively worse, turning from asphalt to packed dirt, and my car—a 1996 Honda Civic with approximately 180,000 miles on it—climbed higher into red rock country. We had no cell service. The map we were using was seven years old. We had maybe a quarter tank of gas.

And instead of panicking, I remember feeling this strange sense of liberation. There was no way to contact anyone. No way to check directions. No way to optimize our route or update our arrival time. We had somehow slipped out of the network, become unreachable, and the only way forward was to keep driving until something made sense. We found a gas station thirty miles later, run by a woman who'd lived in that location for forty-three years and clearly enjoyed our sheepishness immensely. She gave us proper directions, we bought some excellent fry bread, and we got to Flagstaff by evening.

The experience stayed with me. Not because it was harrowing or even particularly interesting in retrospect, but because of that quality of being unmoored. Of not knowing where I was, and slowly making peace with that fact. There's a particular silence that comes with true lostness—not uncomfortable silence, but the kind where you stop looking for an answer and start looking at the landscape instead.

Lately, I wonder if we've engineered lostness out of our lives intentionally. We've made it impossible to be lost in any meaningful way. You have a smartphone with a GPS that can locate you within fifteen feet. You have cloud storage that remembers everywhere you've been. You have social media that tracks your movements through geotagged photos. The very concept of being properly, thoroughly lost has become almost perverse—something that requires deliberately throwing away your phone or driving into a dead zone.

And maybe that's fine. Maybe getting lost is like smallpox—something humanity is better off having eliminated. But I don't think so. I think we've lost something in the process, and it's hard to name exactly what.

There's a certain kind of attention that gets activated when you don't know where you are. You start noticing things differently. The quality of light changes when you're paying attention to it rather than just walking through it. You notice which plants grow in certain areas, what the rocks look like, whether the road is climbing or descending. You notice other people differently too—whether they seem friendly, whether they might help, what they might want. You become more alert, more present, because the world is no longer a series of way-stations between meaningful destinations.

I've been thinking about this partly because I've noticed how much of my life has become destination-oriented. I move through days with a series of tasks and goals, each with clear endpoints. Finish the work, go to the store, write the email, attend the meeting. The intermediate spaces—the actual experiences of moving through time—have become something to optimize away. I listen to podcasts or audiobooks to fill them. I multitask. I try to make them "count" for something, rather than simply experiencing them as they are.

There's something deeply unsatisfying about this, something that leaves me feeling rushed even when I'm not actually rushing anywhere. And I've wondered recently whether what I'm actually missing is permission to be lost, or at least to move through the world without knowing exactly where I'm going, and to be okay with that.

This connects, I think, to the broader way we've structured modern life around certainty and predictability. We want to know what's going to happen. We want to reduce surprise and uncertainty. We make plans and schedules. We research restaurants before we go to them. We read reviews. We watch trailers. We listen to podcasts that tell us what's going to happen in the books we haven't read yet, somehow convinced this will enhance our enjoyment. We've built entire systems to minimize the possibility of encountering something we're unprepared for.

And again, maybe some of this is good. It's probably better to know that a restaurant is sanitary before eating there. It's useful to have some idea of how to get where you're going. But somewhere along the way, we seem to have decided that all uncertainty is bad, that surprise is something to eliminate rather than something to be open to.

I think about this when I walk around my neighborhood. I know exactly where every store is. I know the fastest route to everywhere I regularly go. I've probably walked the same three paths through the neighborhood hundreds of times. And while they're pleasant walks, they're also deeply familiar in a way that makes it hard to actually see them anymore. The detail has worn smooth from repetition. I'm not really walking these routes so much as executing them, watching them unfold along predetermined patterns.

The other day I deliberately took a wrong turn just to see where it would go. It led to a small pocket park I'd never noticed before, tucked between two buildings, with a bench and some flowering plum trees. There was nobody there. I sat on the bench for twenty minutes and did nothing, which is increasingly rare. And it was lovely, that small accidental discovery.

This is the thing about getting lost, even in small ways: it requires admitting that you don't know something. In a culture that valorizes expertise and knowledge, that requires a certain amount of humility. We're supposed to know things. We're supposed to have our lives figured out, our paths clear, our destinations set. To say "I don't know where I'm going" starts to feel like a failure, when really it could be the beginning of an actual experience.

I've been thinking too about the relationship between lostness and creativity. There's probably research on this that I haven't read, but in my own experience, some of my best thinking has happened when I'm not trying to think about anything in particular. When I'm wandering. When I'm not sure where I'm going next. There's a particular quality of mind that emerges when you're not tightly focused on a destination, when you can notice things sideways, make unexpected connections.

Some of my favorite writers and artists seem to have had a capacity for this kind of productive lostness. They'd go on walks and not know where they were going. They'd follow tangents. They'd notice something random and let it completely derail their day. They gave themselves permission to be lost, to wander, to follow curiosity rather than schedule. And this wandering somehow fed their work, gave it a quality of genuine discovery rather than execution.

By contrast, there's something anxiety-inducing about the "optimization culture" that's come to dominate so much of how people approach their lives and work. Everything is quantified. Every minute is optimized for some kind of output. You're supposed to be always improving, always working toward something, always aware of your metrics and your progress. There's no room for lostness in this framework, no room for following a thought just to see where it goes, no room for the productive chaos of genuine exploration.

I don't know how to fix this, or if it's even a problem that needs fixing. Certainly, some optimization is necessary. I'm not advocating that we all abandon calendars and responsibility. But I do think there's something worth questioning in how completely we've eliminated lostness from our lives, how we've decided that every moment should be productive, every action purposeful, every experience optimized.

Because here's the thing about lostness: it has a quality of surrender in it. When you're truly lost, you can't be in control. You have to adapt to circumstances rather than imposing your will on them. You have to pay attention, not because you're checking it off a list of mindfulness practices, but because you actually need to know what's around you. You have to be willing to ask for help, to admit not knowing, to change your plans based on what you find.

There's something deeply human about that, I think. Something that gets lost when we're always in control, always on schedule, always confident that we know exactly where we're going.

The other thing about getting lost is that it teaches you something about scale. When you're lost, you realize how much of the world exists that you're not aware of, how many small roads and hidden places and unexpected things there are. Your confident sense of understanding how things work gets a little cracked. You realize you're smaller and less in control than you thought you were. Which sounds depressing, but I actually find it oddly freeing.

There's a particular kind of arrogance that comes from always knowing where you are, from always being in control, from having optimized your life so thoroughly that nothing can surprise you. It's an arrogance I fall into often, that sense that I've figured things out, that I understand how the world works, that I have my trajectory set and I'm executing the plan. Getting lost cracks that arrogance in a useful way.

I think that's why so many people find travel refreshing, incidentally. It's not just the novelty of being somewhere different, though that helps. It's that travel, especially to places where you don't speak the language or understand the customs, forces you to be lost in a temporary, controlled way. You have permission to not understand things. Permission to be confused. Permission to move more slowly because you have to pay attention. And there's relief in that permission.

What if we gave ourselves that permission more often, even in the contexts of our normal lives? What if we occasionally chose the route we didn't know? What if we sometimes didn't have a plan? What if we allowed for the possibility of being lost, not as a failure state to be fixed immediately, but as a temporary condition to be explored?

I'm not sure what that would look like for most people. We have real obligations and schedules and places we need to be. But maybe it doesn't have to be grand. Maybe it's just taking a walk without deciding where you're going first. Maybe it's following a rabbit hole in conversation instead of checking the time. Maybe it's reading something that interests you without being sure what you're going to do with that knowledge. Maybe it's sitting in a park and doing nothing for twenty minutes.

The small surrenders. The tiny permissions to not be completely in control.

Because there's something about the human mind that seems to need those spaces—the unstructured time, the undirected attention, the gentle lostness of not knowing exactly what comes next. We talk about needing vacation and downtime and relaxation, but maybe what we actually need is permission to be lost, to wander, to let our attention go where it wants to go rather than where we think it should go.

The culture we've built is very good at making us productive. It's very good at getting us efficiently from point A to point B. It's very good at helping us accomplish things. But I'm not sure it's particularly good at helping us actually live—at paying attention to the world around us, at noticing details, at following curiosity, at being surprised.

And I think we lose something important in that optimization. Some essential part of being human that can only emerge when we're not in control, when we're not sure where we're going, when we're willing to be lost.

So maybe the radical act, in a world that's become so thoroughly mapped and planned and optimized, is simply to get lost once in a while. Not recklessly. Not in ways that make you truly unsafe. But in small ways. To admit that you don't know where you're going and to be okay with that. To notice what you find along the way. To let your attention wander. To follow a thought or a road just to see where it leads.

In a life that's become increasingly scheduled and optimized and certain, getting lost might be one of the last truly wild things we can still do. And maybe we need that wildness. Maybe that's where we find ourselves.
